hidden_cases.rationale: The deliverable's second obligation is an explicit assertion that no replacement was performed. The tool has a -o flag that writes a file. Nobody asked what happens when the output path is one of the input paths.
hidden_cases.construction: Wrote a 43-byte victim.md containing '# Routing / Routed via Operator D on 18 Aug.', then ran the census with that same file as both the input path and the -o target.
hidden_cases.observed_output_verbatim:
exit=0
   input file preserved: False
   the input file now contains the census report itself: occurrence_count=1
   ...while that same report asserts: 'No alias replacement was performed; inputs were read-only.'
   ...and replacement_performed=False
   original 43 bytes -> now 397 bytes; alias text still present: True
hidden_cases.interpretation: The input file is destroyed and replaced by the census report, and the report that overwrote it asserts in its own body that inputs were read-only. Both replacement_performed and replacement_assertion are literal constants in the returned dict, computed from nothing, so the assertion cannot fail no matter what the process actually did to the filesystem. The deliverable asks the census to assert that no replacement was performed; what it ships is a sentence that says so unconditionally. Two caveats in the producer's favour: the alias text survives inside the report's 'text' field so this is not an alias rewrite, and the producer's own run demonstrably did not do this - I reproduced its census byte for byte with no input modified. The defect is that the guarantee is decoration rather than a check.

hidden_cases.rationale: The deliverable says 'every' occurrence. The patterns join words with \s+, so any hyphenated spelling of an alias is unmatched. The question is whether hyphenated spellings actually occur in this repository or only in my imagination.
hidden_cases.construction: First a synthetic variant sweep through census() directly, then a full pass over the c5 tree counting real occurrences of Operator-D, Claude-extension and Claude browser-operator forms that the producer's own ALIAS_PATTERNS cannot match, excluding the unit's own census.json output.

The patterns handle whitespace variation well - multiple spaces and tabs both match, and the optional 'Chrome' infix is a thoughtful touch - but hyphenation was not considered, and AGENTS.md rule 4 explicitly extends the prohibition to 'similar phrases'.

One hundred and forty-five genuine occurrences across 48 files are absent, and the largest single omission is dispatch/ with 84 - which is precisely the routing-surface directory the alias prohibition exists to govern, and which contains files named CLAUDE_EXTENSION_REFERENCE_DISPATCH and OPERATOR_D_REFERENCE_UPDATE. hidden_cases.rationale: The deliverable requires the 'surrounding field' for each occurrence. That is easy on flat JSON and easy to get wrong elsewhere.
hidden_cases.construction: Fed the census five shapes: nested JSONL, YAML-style indentation, CSV, unstructured text, and markdown with a heading two levels up.
hidden_cases.interpretation: This part is done well. Nested JSON resolves to the innermost key rather than the outermost, YAML-style keys resolve correctly despite no YAML parser being involved, markdown falls back to the nearest preceding heading rather than the document title, and genuinely unstructured lines are labelled honestly as 'unstructured-line' instead of guessing. CSV degrades to unstructured, which is the truthful answer for a format with no field on the line.

hidden_cases.rationale: The census swallows UnicodeDecodeError and OSError with a bare continue. A silent skip is invisible in the output, and the report has no counter for it.

hidden_cases.rationale: The commission's stub-substitution test. Both of the producer's tests assert fixed expected values against fixtures they wrote themselves, so the question is whether an implementation that never reads its input can satisfy them.
hidden_cases.construction: Two stubs in place of legacy_alias_census.py with the test file unchanged: (1) a stateless constant stub returning one canned occurrence; (2) a stub that reads no file at all and returns canned values chosen by call ordinal, since unittest runs these two tests in a fixed alphabetical order.
hidden_cases.observed_output_verbatim:

   input-ignoring stub: exit=0 (STILL PASSES -> VACUOUS)
hidden_cases.interpretation: Partially vacuous, and I want the distinction on the record because it is not the flat vacuity I found in unit 024. A single constant stub does fail, because the two tests expect different enclosing_field values, so the suite has some discrimination. But an implementation that opens no file whatsoever passes both, because every expected value is hardcoded in the test and nothing ties the output back to the fixture's content. The tests never assert, for example, that the recorded 'text' field equals the fixture line, which would have been one line and would have defeated my stub. Note what does the real work here: the read-only check in the first test is genuine - it compares the fixture's bytes before and after - and my HC-A shows that check is the only reason the read-only claim has any teeth at all.

The manifest evidence line names the roots it scanned rather than implying whole-repository coverage - 'read AGENTS.md, operations, state, instructions, templates, _transport, packs and modules and recorded 129 occurrences across 50 files' - and both the 129 and the 50 are exactly right, which I confirmed independently. reproducibility_check: The best in my set. The committed 61015-byte census.json regenerates byte for byte with identical SHA-256 from a fresh process on a clean extraction of the commit, and a separate two-file determinism probe was also byte-identical across processes.
vacuous_test_qualifier: Partial, not total. A stateless constant stub fails the suite; a stub that never opens its input file passes it. Recorded as a finding but materially weaker than unit 024's, and offset by the byte-exact real-repository reproduction which no stub could fake.
divergence_reason: The frozen deliverable requires a census of EVERY legacy alias occurrence, and two independent measurements show the census is not that. By scope, running the producer's own tool over the whole c5 tree finds 270 occurrence sites against the 125 recorded - 145 omitted across 48 files, including 84 in dispatch/, the routing-surface directory the alias prohibition is chiefly about. By detection, 21 real occurrences in 14 files are unmatchable by the producer's patterns because hyphenated spellings like Operator-D and Claude-extension are joined with \s+, and several of those sit inside state/ which the census did scan - so this is a miss within the declared scope, not merely a narrower scope. Separately, the deliverable's assertion that no replacement was performed is a hardcoded literal: aiming -o at an input path destroys that file and rewrites it with a report stating that inputs were read-only. I record NOT_YET rather than FAIL because the hypothesis as worded is true and was honestly demonstrated - aliases were censused as evidence and no replacement was performed in the producer's actual run, which I confirmed by regenerating census.json byte for byte. The unit is an incomplete instance of a correct idea, not a false claim.
disposition_reason: Rejected on completeness against a deliverable whose operative word is 'every', with the clear statement that the census which does exist is real, honest and immediately reusable. The strengths are substantial and worth recording plainly: this is the only unit in my twenty whose primary evidence artifact regenerated byte for byte - 61015 bytes, SHA-256 a322f942..., 129 occurrences across 50 real repository files, zero record-level divergence from my independent run - so nothing here is invented and the evidence is real-repository rather than synthetic. The enclosing-field extraction is better than it needed to be, resolving nested JSON to the innermost key and markdown to the nearest preceding heading, and the manifest's evidence line discloses which roots were scanned instead of implying full coverage. What blocks acceptance is that a census of prohibited routing aliases omits the dispatch tree entirely, where 84 occurrences sit in files literally named CLAUDE_EXTENSION_REFERENCE_DISPATCH and OPERATOR_D_REFERENCE_UPDATE, and that 21 further occurrences are undetectable anywhere because hyphenated spellings were never considered. The read-only guarantee is a constant string rather than a check, and I falsified it by pointing the output at an input. None of these is a redesign: widen the roots to the whole tree, allow [-_ ] between alias words, compare a hash of every input before and after so the assertion is earned, and add a skipped-file counter. The existing 129 records stay valid and the re-run should reproduce them as a subset.
followups_for_coordinator: BLOCKING for re-run: census the whole tree, or state the excluded roots as an explicit exclusion list with a reason. Reviewer-observed: the producer's own tool over the full c5 tree finds 270 occurrence sites versus 125 recorded, with 145 omitted across 48 files - dispatch 84, commissions 24, receipts 21, workstreams 6, handoff 4, scripts 4, handover 2.

BLOCKING for re-run: allow [-_ ] rather than only \s+ between alias words. Reviewer-observed: 21 real occurrences in 14 files are unmatchable, 12 of Claude-extension and 9 of Operator-D, and some are inside state/ which the census did scan.

Make the no-replacement assertion earned rather than declared: hash every input before and after and derive replacement_performed from the comparison. At minimum refuse an output path that is also an input path.

Add a skipped-file counter to the report, as unit 003 does with skipped_binary_artifacts. Non-UTF-8 files are currently skipped invisibly, so a reader cannot tell whether the census passed over nothing or a great deal.
